Party Fractures and Voter Anger Topple Republicans in a Conservative Bastion
 
Plus, Mississippi elects its first Black senator since Reconstruction, and Nvidia prepares to oust Jensen Huang
 
 
JESSE BARBER FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

South Carolina’s Greenville County is the spiritual home of the modern Republican Party, the cornerstone of the GOP’s Southern Wall and the wellspring of every conservative wave of the past half-century—from the Moral Majority to MAGA.

 

So it was striking when Trey Walker, the longtime chief of staff to Republican Gov. Henry McMaster, told our reporters that his party’s drubbing there was deserved.

 

Democrat Annie Andrews won the Senate seat that Lindsey Graham held for more than two decades, carrying not only the state but, astonishingly, Greenville County itself. The upset underscores the changing fabric of a county that has become an emblem of the New South and a magnet for transplants, including conservative retirees from blue states.

 

The race also turned on local fractures within the Republican Party that, in better political times, might have been manageable.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after he had two extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee.

 

• Scott Colom won a long-shot bid to oust Mississippi’s Republican incumbent senator.

 

• Eleven Democratic House members weren’t present for the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote, potentially enough to have swung the result their way, angering activists and bewildering party colleagues.

 

• United Airlines is banning personal artificial-intelligence assistants from booking flights. Meanwhile, Big Tech wants everyone to use an AI agent—but who shoulders the cost?

 

• Advances in ballistic missiles have allowed Iran and the Houthis to hit foes across the Mideast. The spread of these weapons means military doctrines will need profound change, writes Yaroslav Trofimov.

 

• Tensions between veterinarians, staff and pet owners are running high as prices skyrocket, pets become more pampered and doctors have to deliver harsh news—like telling an owner their dog is too fat.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

A mystery businessman introduced Jensen Huang to his paramour—her husband.

 

Before the affair that engulfed Nvidia in scandal, co-founder Jensen Huang was introduced to his future romantic interest, Alice Huang, by a Chinese businessman he’d known for a decade, Kang Wei. Kang also happened to be Alice Huang’s husband, said people who know the couple. For two years, Kang appeared to accept his wife’s romantic relationship with the Nvidia CEO and spoke openly of their closeness, these people said. Sometimes Kang told associates, half-jokingly, that she was a personal assistant to Jensen Huang, they said. The introduction to the CEO at the center of the global AI boom is the clearest example of how Kang and Alice Huang leveraged personal connections to further an array of business ventures in China, Singapore, Taiwan and elsewhere, reports Lingling Wei.

 

5.

 

Meet the real-estate billionaire spending a fortune to slow down aging.

 

Time might be the one thing money can’t buy. It hasn’t stopped Larry Connor from paying to slow it down. The billionaire real-estate investor’s Miamisburg, Ohio, offices regularly host strength trainers, yoga instructors and massage therapists. Roughly 15 professionals help keep him in peak physical and mental condition. Connor’s investments have paid dividends. The energetic 76-year-old proudly showcases a chart tracking how his cholesterol levels have edged lower in the past decade. He has trekked through Alaskan wilderness and completed a 17-day mission to the International Space Station that cost tens of millions of dollars. The wealthy are spending big on everything from concierge doctors to specialized longevity practitioners promising treatments to help them live longer, reports Gunjan Banerji.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

This shipping lane is now the world’s deadliest. It isn’t Hormuz.

 
 
DANIEL KISS
 

A series of attacks in the Black Sea has killed more people than strikes on shipping so far in the war between Iran and the U.S., disrupting trade routes and turning up the heat on NATO. Russian forces have targeted commercial ships carrying food exports from Ukraine out into the Black Sea. Ukraine, too, has attacked Russian shipping on the other side of the sea with drones. The strikes have expanded to the waters of Romania and Bulgaria, both members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, in a spate of recent deadly incidents.

That is the value of the vacation AI startup Serval is offering new hires—alongside a $30,000 signing bonus—to fill engineering roles. Despite broader U.S. tech job cuts, intense competition with giants like Anthropic and OpenAI has left top talent with the upper hand.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

WSJ readers share seven lessons about switching to an EV.

 

After our technology columnist Christopher Mims drove the affordable Chevy Bolt through the charging desert of the Deep South, readers shared their own observations about EV benefits—and liabilities. One important takeaway? Charging time vs. gas-pump time isn’t apples-to-apples.
